question: Why fashion marketing specifically, rather than fashion design or fashion buying?
lookingFor: A clear sense of what draws them to the business and storytelling side of fashion rather than the making of it.

bullets: Distinguish marketing from design and buying in their own words
Point to a concrete moment or experience that revealed the pull toward brand and consumer thinking
Show they understand marketing is about people and meaning, not just clothes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I love clothes but I've always been more interested in why people buy them than in how they're made. Running my school's fashion show, I ended up doing all the social media promotion instead of the styling, and I found I cared more about how we told the story than what was on the runway. That's when I realised I wanted the business and communication side, not the design side. Marketing lets me sit at the point where a brand's identity meets a real person's choice, and that's the puzzle I want to keep working on.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love fashion' without distinguishing the discipline
Implying design is easier or less serious than marketing
No concrete experience backing the claim
followUps: What part of marketing specifically excites you most: branding, advertising, or consumer research?

question: Why do you want to study Fashion Marketing at this university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course rather than generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific module, industry placement, or faculty strength
Connect it to a personal goal or project
Show awareness of what makes this course distinct from others
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a live brief module where students work directly with a retail partner on a real campaign, and that hands-on structure is exactly how I learn best. I ran a small resale Instagram account through school and the thing I struggled with most was translating a brand idea into an actual customer response, which is precisely what that module is built to teach. I also looked at where your graduates end up, and the mix of buying, brand, and digital roles tells me the course keeps its options open rather than funnelling everyone into one path. That flexibility matters to me because I'm still working out which corner of marketing I want to specialise in.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any fashion course
Citing only league table rankings
Not naming anything specific about the course structure
followUps: What would you want to get out of a live brief or placement, specifically?

question: What first drew you to the fashion industry?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story rather than a vague love of clothes.

bullets: Pick one real moment or experience, not a general statement
Show what specifically caught their attention
Link it forward to their current interest in marketing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It started when I noticed how differently my two favourite brands talked to me even though they sold almost the same product. One made me feel like I was joining something, the other just listed features, and I couldn't stop thinking about why that difference worked on me. I started following brand strategists and marketing accounts to understand the mechanics behind it. That curiosity about the feeling behind a purchase is what pulled me from just liking fashion to wanting to study how it's sold.

commonMistakes: A vague 'I've always loved clothes' with nothing specific
Describing pure consumption with no reflection
Not connecting the story back to marketing
followUps: Has that interest changed or narrowed since then?

question: What's the difference between fashion marketing and fashion merchandising, as you understand it?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate grasp of the two functions and how they work together.

bullets: Define marketing as building demand and brand perception
Define merchandising as planning what product goes where, in what quantity, at what price and time
Note that the two have to work closely together to succeed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Marketing is about building the story and the demand, so advertising, brand positioning, social media, getting people to want the product. Merchandising is more about getting the right product to the right place at the right time and price, so planning stock, ranges, and how it moves through stores. They obviously overlap a lot, because a merchandiser deciding what to stock needs to know what marketing has promised customers, and marketing can't sell what merchandising hasn't planned for. I find that overlap interesting because it's where a lot of real strategy actually happens.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as interchangeable
Defining only one of the two functions
No mention of how they interact
followUps: Which of the two would you rather work closer to, and why?

question: Can you walk me through the 4 Ps of marketing using a fashion brand as an example?
lookingFor: Correct recall of product, price, place, promotion, applied concretely to a real brand.

bullets: Name all four Ps correctly: product, price, place, promotion
Apply each to one specific brand rather than speaking abstractly
Show the Ps working together, not as isolated boxes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'll use a brand like Uniqlo. Product is the basics-focused, function-driven clothing itself, like their HeatTech range. Price is accessible but not the cheapest, positioned as good value rather than a bargain. Place is their own flagship stores plus online, kept deliberately controlled rather than sold through every retailer. Promotion leans on product innovation and collaborations rather than celebrity glamour, which fits the whole functional, no-fuss identity. What I like about that example is how consistent all four Ps are with each other, which is really the whole point of the framework.

commonMistakes: Forgetting one of the four Ps
Staying abstract with no real brand example
Contradicting the brand's actual positioning
followUps: Is there a fifth P you think matters for fashion specifically, like people or packaging?

question: Which fashion brand do you think markets itself best, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, well-reasoned brand pick with real analysis, not just enthusiasm.

bullets: Name one brand and explain what specifically works
Point to identity, consistency, or audience understanding, not just aesthetics
Show awareness of who the brand is targeting and why it lands
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd pick Glossier, even though it's technically beauty rather than clothing, because the way it built a community-first identity is a masterclass I think fashion brands are still copying. They turned customers into the product photographers by building the whole visual language around real bathroom shelfies rather than studio shoots, which made the brand feel co-owned by its audience. That trust is why people forgive the higher price and keep coming back. It taught me that consistent identity can matter more than budget in building loyalty.

commonMistakes: Naming a brand with no explanation of why it markets well
Confusing good product with good marketing
Picking the most famous brand rather than the most thoughtful example
followUps: What would you change about that brand's marketing if you were advising them?

question: Fast fashion brands are hugely profitable but widely criticised on sustainability grounds. As a future marketer, how would you think about that tension?
lookingFor: Balanced, structured reasoning that doesn't dodge the ethical tension or lapse into empty idealism.

bullets: Acknowledge both the commercial reality and the genuine environmental and labour concerns
Reason through where marketing sits in that tension, rather than claiming it's someone else's problem
Land on a considered personal position, even a provisional one
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think marketers get to say sustainability is someone else's department, because marketing is exactly what creates the demand for constant new drops in the first place. At the same time, fast fashion exists because it genuinely serves people who can't afford or don't want to spend more, so I'm wary of a purely moralising answer. What I'd want to work on is marketing that's honest about trade-offs and pushes brands toward slower, more durable ranges without pretending that's costless for the business. I don't think I have a clean answer, but I'd rather work somewhere trying to shift the model than somewhere ignoring the question.

commonMistakes: Condemning fast fashion outright with no nuance about affordability
Defending it purely on commercial grounds with no ethical reflection
Refusing to take any position at all
followUps: Can you name a brand you think is handling that tension reasonably well?

question: If you were launching a new streetwear label, how would you go about defining its target market?
lookingFor: A structured approach to segmentation that goes beyond age and gender into behaviour and values.

bullets: Move beyond basic demographics into lifestyle, values, and buying behaviour
Mention research methods like social listening, surveys, or competitor audience analysis
Show that a target market shapes product, price, and channel choices, not just advertising
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't start with age and gender alone, because two eighteen-year-olds can have completely different relationships with streetwear. I'd want to understand behaviour and values instead, so things like whether they follow specific sneaker culture, how much they care about limited drops, and where they actually discover new brands, probably through social listening and looking at who engages with similar labels. That research would then shape more than the ad campaign, it would inform pricing, where we sell, and how scarce we make releases. Getting that definition wrong early is expensive, because everything downstream depends on it.

commonMistakes: Defining a target market only by age and income bracket
Treating target market definition as a marketing-only decision
No mention of any research method
followUps: How would you validate that your assumed target market is right before spending on a campaign?

question: How do you think social media and influencer marketing have changed how fashion brands operate?
lookingFor: An informed view of the shift from top-down advertising to influencer and community-driven marketing, with awareness of its risks.

bullets: Explain the shift from controlled advertising to influencer and community-driven trust
Mention specific mechanics like micro-influencers, UGC, or trend cycles on platforms like TikTok
Show awareness of the risks: authenticity, saturation, or brand safety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Brands used to control the story almost entirely through a handful of ad campaigns, but now a lot of that trust is borrowed from creators the audience already follows. What interests me is how far it's gone toward micro-influencers, because a smaller creator with a tight, loyal following often converts better than a huge name people don't really trust. TikTok in particular has compressed trend cycles so fast that brands now have to be reactive in a way traditional marketing never required. The risk is that it can feel manufactured if the partnership isn't genuine, so I think the brands doing it well are the ones being selective rather than chasing every trend.

commonMistakes: Treating influencer marketing as just paying someone famous to post
No mention of any risk or downside
Vague comments about 'social media is important' with no mechanism explained
followUps: Can you think of a case where influencer marketing backfired for a brand?

question: Tell us about a fashion marketing campaign you've seen recently that you thought was particularly effective.
lookingFor: Genuine, current engagement with the industry and the ability to explain why a campaign worked, not just describe it.

bullets: Name a real, recent campaign with specifics
Explain the strategic reasoning behind why it worked, not just describe it
Connect it to the brand's broader positioning or audience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The campaign that stuck with me was Dove's ongoing Real Beauty work extending into how they've pushed back on AI-generated bodies in advertising. It's not new as a concept, but the timing was smart because it directly named a fear a lot of people were already feeling about digitally perfected images. It worked because it wasn't just a nice message, it was tied to an actual commitment they'd made about how they'd use imagery going forward, so it felt backed by policy rather than just a slogan. I think the lesson is that a campaign lands harder when the message and the brand's actual behaviour match.

commonMistakes: Naming a campaign with no explanation of why it worked
Choosing something outdated or generic with no personal reflection
Confusing a viral moment with strategic effectiveness
followUps: Was there a campaign recently that you thought missed the mark?

question: How does marketing a luxury fashion brand differ from marketing a mass-market one?
lookingFor: Understanding of scarcity, exclusivity, and pricing psychology as distinct from volume-driven mass marketing.

bullets: Explain luxury marketing's reliance on scarcity, heritage, and exclusivity
Contrast with mass-market's reliance on accessibility, volume, and frequent promotion
Note the different relationship each has with discounting and distribution
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Luxury marketing generally works by making the product feel harder to get, not easier, so heritage, craftsmanship stories, and limited distribution all reinforce that scarcity, and you rarely see luxury brands discounting because it would undercut the whole premise. Mass-market marketing is closer to the opposite, competing on accessibility, frequent new stock, and promotions that get people back in the door often. Even the store experience reflects it, a luxury boutique wants you to feel invited in, while a mass-market store wants high footfall and turnover. I find it a useful reminder that the same discipline of marketing can pull in almost opposite directions depending on the positioning.

commonMistakes: Saying luxury marketing is just 'more expensive advertising'
No mention of scarcity or exclusivity as a mechanism
Ignoring the different attitude toward discounting
followUps: What happens to a luxury brand's identity when it discounts heavily?

question: What do you understand about how fashion trend forecasting works?
lookingFor: A basic but correct understanding that forecasting blends data, cultural observation, and industry signals rather than guesswork.

bullets: Mention that forecasting draws on runway shows, street style, and cultural or social shifts
Note the role of data tools and sales trend tracking alongside human judgement
Show awareness of the long lead time between forecasting and product hitting shelves
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I understand, forecasters aren't just guessing, they're combining runway shows and trade shows with street style observation and broader cultural signals, like what's happening in music or film that might influence colour or silhouette choices. There's also a data side now, with tools tracking search trends and social conversation to spot things gaining momentum earlier. What surprised me learning about it is the lead time, because forecasters are often working eighteen months to two years ahead of the season a trend actually appears in stores. That gap is what makes it feel like such a high-stakes, almost intuitive skill alongside the data.

commonMistakes: Describing forecasting as pure guesswork or personal taste
No mention of any real source of forecasting information
Ignoring the long lead times involved
followUps: Do you think forecasting is getting easier or harder with social media speeding up trend cycles?

question: How much responsibility do you think fashion marketers bear for the sustainability problems in the industry's supply chain?
lookingFor: Nuanced reasoning about marketing's role in shaping demand and messaging, without either dodging responsibility or overclaiming power marketers don't have.

bullets: Distinguish what marketing can influence (demand, messaging, transparency) from what it can't (manufacturing decisions)
Address greenwashing as a real risk marketers specifically create
Reach a considered, non-evasive position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Marketers don't design the supply chain, so I don't think all the responsibility sits with us, but we do control the story that gets told about it, and that's exactly where greenwashing happens when a brand oversells a small sustainable capsule while the rest of the range stays unchanged. I think the honest responsibility marketers have is to refuse to overstate progress and to push internally for claims that actually hold up to scrutiny. It's uncomfortable because that sometimes means telling a less flattering story than a brand wants. I'd rather be the person in the room insisting the marketing matches the reality than the person writing around it.

commonMistakes: Claiming marketing has no responsibility because manufacturing decisions sit elsewhere
Overclaiming that marketers can single-handedly fix supply chain issues
Not mentioning greenwashing at all
followUps: Can you give an example of what you'd consider greenwashing in a real campaign?

question: What does a fashion buyer actually do, as far as you understand it?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate picture of the buying function and how it connects commercial decisions to what customers see in store.

bullets: Explain buying as selecting and committing to stock based on sales data and trend input
Mention the commercial pressure: balancing risk, budget, and trend timing
Note the link between buying decisions and what marketing then has to sell
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A buyer decides what actually goes into the range each season, working from sales data, trend research, and a set budget, then negotiates with suppliers and commits to quantities months before the stock arrives. It's a genuinely risky job because getting the mix wrong, ordering too much of something that doesn't sell or missing a trend, has real financial consequences. What I find interesting is how tightly buying and marketing have to stay in sync, because marketing can't credibly promote a trend the buyer didn't actually stock, and a buyer's decisions only pay off if marketing gets customers excited about them.

commonMistakes: Confusing buying with personal shopping or styling
No mention of budget or commercial risk
Treating buying as disconnected from marketing
followUps: Why do you think buying and marketing sometimes clash inside a company?

question: Why do you think so many fashion brands have shifted toward direct-to-consumer selling instead of relying on department stores and retailers?
lookingFor: Understanding of the commercial and marketing incentives behind DTC, including margin, data, and brand control.

bullets: Mention margin: cutting out the retailer middleman
Mention data: owning the customer relationship and purchase data directly
Mention brand control: presenting the product exactly as intended rather than through a retailer's lens
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Selling through a department store means giving up a chunk of margin and also giving up control over how the product actually gets presented, since a retailer's shelf or website treats every brand fairly similarly. Going direct means a brand keeps more of the revenue and, maybe more importantly now, owns the customer data, so they know exactly who's buying, when, and what else they're browsing. It also means the brand controls its own story completely, from the site design to the email flow after purchase. The trade-off is they lose the retailer's existing footfall and have to build their own audience from scratch, which is genuinely hard and expensive.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning margin without data or brand control
Ignoring the trade-off, like the cost of building an audience from scratch
Confusing DTC with just having a website
followUps: What's a risk a brand takes on by going fully direct-to-consumer?

question: What's the actual purpose of Fashion Week from a marketing point of view?
lookingFor: Understanding that Fashion Week functions as press, buyer, and brand-image event, not just a public show.

bullets: Identify the primary audiences: press, buyers, and increasingly, social media and consumers
Explain that it sets seasonal narrative and trend direction for the industry
Note how its role has shifted with livestreaming and direct-to-consumer social coverage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Fashion Week isn't really built for the general public, it's aimed first at press and buyers who are deciding what to write about and what to order for the season ahead. It's where a brand sets its story for the season, the mood, the silhouette direction, the cultural references, all the things that then trickle into everyone else's marketing and merchandising decisions. What's changed is that with livestreaming and social media, ordinary consumers now watch shows in real time too, so shows increasingly have to work as content in their own right, not just as a trade event. That double audience, industry insiders and the public at once, makes designing a show a genuinely tricky marketing problem.

commonMistakes: Describing it purely as a public entertainment event
Not mentioning buyers or press as the core audience
No acknowledgment of how social media has changed its role
followUps: Do you think Fashion Week is becoming less relevant with social media setting trends faster?

subtopic: Data and analytics in marketing decisions
question: How do you think fashion brands use data to make marketing decisions?
lookingFor: Awareness that marketing decisions are increasingly data-informed, with concrete examples beyond vague mentions of 'big data'.

bullets: Give a concrete example, such as A/B testing ads, tracking conversion by channel, or personalised email
Note the balance between data and creative or intuitive judgement
Show awareness that data informs, but doesn't fully replace, brand strategy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A concrete example is how brands A/B test almost everything now, like running two versions of an ad image or email subject line to see which actually converts better before committing budget to one. They also segment customers by past purchase behaviour to personalise what gets recommended or emailed to them. I don't think data replaces the creative judgement about what a brand should stand for, but it does tell you quickly whether an idea is landing with real customers rather than just internally. I like that mix, because it means marketing isn't just opinion, there's a way to actually test whether you're right.

commonMistakes: Vague statements about 'using big data' with no concrete example
Implying data replaces creative or brand judgement entirely
Confusing data analytics with market research surveys only
followUps: What's a decision you think should stay based on creative judgement rather than data?

question: Take two competing fashion brands you know well. How do they position themselves differently to win the same customer?
lookingFor: The ability to do real comparative brand analysis, identifying meaningfully different positioning rather than surface differences.

bullets: Pick two genuine competitors and identify their core positioning difference, not just style
Point to consistent signals across product, price, and communication that reinforce each position
Show understanding of who each brand is actually trying to win over
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd compare Nike and New Balance, since they compete for a lot of the same footwear customer but position very differently. Nike sells aspiration and performance mythology, built around athlete stories and the idea of pushing your limits, and everything from its pricing to its ad tone reinforces that intensity. New Balance has leaned into a quieter, almost anti-hype positioning, dad-shoe-turned-cool, appealing to people who want quality and heritage without the loud branding. Both are chasing a similar customer base, but one wins through emotional intensity and the other through understated credibility, and I think that contrast is a genuinely useful case study in how two brands can succeed in the same market with almost opposite tones.

commonMistakes: Comparing brands that aren't real competitors for the same customer
Describing only aesthetic differences without positioning logic
One-sided analysis that doesn't explain how both brands actually win customers
followUps: Which of the two positioning strategies would be harder to maintain long term, and why?

question: How would you describe your own personal style, and what does it say about you as a future marketer?
lookingFor: Genuine self-reflection connecting personal taste to a broader understanding of identity and marketing, not just a fashion description.

bullets: Describe personal style specifically, not just 'casual' or 'I like fashion'
Reflect on what that style choice signals or communicates
Connect it, lightly, to their interest in how clothing communicates identity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd call my style quietly maximalist, I wear mostly neutral basics but I'll always have one loud piece, a bag or a shoe, that does the talking. I think that's actually a fair description of how I approach most things, understated until there's a reason not to be. Thinking about why I dress that way is honestly what got me curious about marketing in the first place, because clothing is one of the few things we choose every single day that says something about us without us saying a word.

commonMistakes: A vague 'I like to be comfortable' with no real description
Treating the question as purely about aesthetics with no reflection
Overexplaining brands worn rather than describing actual style
followUps: Has your style changed a lot over the last few years, and what changed it?

question: What fashion or marketing publications, podcasts, or accounts do you follow to stay current?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with the industry beyond consumer-level following.

bullets: Name specific, credible sources, not just generic fashion Instagram
Mention something specific and recent they learned or found interesting from one
Show a habit of following the industry, not a one-off search before the interview
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Business of Fashion regularly, and I've been following their coverage of how brands are handling the shift away from third-party cookies for ad targeting, which is a real headache for a lot of digital-first labels. I also listen to a marketing podcast that occasionally interviews brand founders, and one episode with a DTC skincare founder talking about customer acquisition costs actually changed how I think about why brands push so hard for repeat purchases rather than just new customers. It's become a genuine habit rather than something I did just to prepare for interviews.

commonMistakes: Naming only consumer fashion magazines with no business or marketing angle
Vague name-dropping with no detail about what they actually learned
Sounding like the research was done the night before the interview
followUps: What's the most surprising thing you've learned from following the industry this way?

question: Tell us about any experience you have that's relevant to fashion marketing, whether that's retail work, a personal project, or something else.
lookingFor: Concrete, reflective experience with a specific lesson taken from it, however small the experience.

bullets: Describe one concrete experience rather than a list of unconnected activities
Explain the specific role they played and a decision they made
Draw out a genuine lesson or insight from it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked part-time on the shop floor at a mid-size clothing retailer for a year, and what stood out to me was how much the in-store displays actually changed what people picked up, way more than I expected from something that seemed like just decoration. I started paying attention to which mannequin outfits got copied by customers and mentioned it to my manager, and we ended up rotating the window display more often, which the manager said did seem to help footfall. It taught me that marketing isn't only campaigns and adverts, a huge amount of it happens quietly at the point of sale, which is something I want to understand properly rather than just observe from behind a till.

commonMistakes: Listing unrelated extracurriculars with no fashion or marketing connection
Describing experience with no specific detail or outcome
No reflection or lesson drawn from the experience
followUps: What would you do differently if you were back in that role now?

question: Imagine you're on the marketing team for a new collection launch, and a week in, sales are far below target. As a student thinking through the problem, what would you want to check first?
lookingFor: Structured, logical problem-solving that separates possible causes before jumping to a fix.

bullets: Resist jumping to a single explanation; lay out a few possible causes first
Distinguish between a product problem, a targeting problem, and a message or channel problem
Show they'd look at data before proposing a solution
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before assuming it's a marketing failure, I'd want to rule out whether it's actually a product or pricing issue, since no amount of messaging fixes a collection people just don't want at that price. If the product itself seems fine, I'd look at where the traffic is coming from and whether people are seeing the campaign at all, versus seeing it but not converting, because those point to completely different fixes, one being reach and the other being message or offer. I'd also check whether we're reaching the audience we actually intended, because a beautiful campaign aimed at the wrong people will always underperform. I think the instinct to immediately increase ad spend without diagnosing which of those it is would be the mistake I'd want to avoid.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to 'spend more on ads' without diagnosis
Assuming it must be a marketing failure without considering product or price
No structured way of separating possible causes
followUps: If it turned out to be a targeting problem, what would you actually do next?

question: Why do you think diversity and inclusion in fashion advertising has become such a prominent issue in the last decade?
lookingFor: An informed view connecting representation to both genuine social change and commercial reality, without sounding rehearsed.

bullets: Connect the shift to broader social movements and consumer expectations, not just brand PR
Acknowledge the commercial dimension honestly, without reducing it to pure cynicism
Show awareness of the difference between genuine inclusion and performative representation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Part of it is that consumers, especially younger ones, expect the brands they support to reflect the world they actually live in, so advertising that only shows one narrow body type or ethnicity increasingly reads as out of touch rather than aspirational. There's also a real commercial logic, since brands that ignored large parts of their potential customer base for years are simply leaving money on the table by not representing them. What I try to watch for is the difference between a brand actually changing who designs, models, and leads campaigns versus one just adding diverse faces to an otherwise unchanged campaign, because customers can usually tell the difference now. I think that scrutiny is a genuinely good thing for the industry even when it's uncomfortable for brands.

commonMistakes: Framing it as purely a PR trend with no genuine social driver
Treating all diverse casting as automatically genuine with no critical eye
Sounding like a rehearsed corporate statement with no personal view
followUps: Can you think of a campaign that felt like performative representation rather than genuine change?

question: Can you explain why a brand might price something at 49 dollars rather than 50, and whether you think that kind of pricing psychology still works?
lookingFor: Understanding of charm pricing and psychological anchoring, along with a genuine opinion on its current effectiveness.

bullets: Explain the mechanism: the left digit effect making 49 read as meaningfully cheaper than 50
Note it's more associated with mass-market and discount positioning than luxury
Offer a genuine view on whether it still works given how price-savvy consumers have become
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's called charm pricing, and it works off what's called the left digit effect, where our brains anchor on the first number we see, so 49 registers as being in the 'forty' range even though it's a single dollar from fifty. It's a technique you see constantly in mass-market and discount retail, but you almost never see it in luxury, because ending a price in .99 undercuts the exact premium feeling luxury pricing is trying to create. I do think it still works at the margins, but I'd guess its effect has weakened as consumers have gotten more price-savvy and used to comparison shopping instantly on their phones. I'd be curious to actually see recent data on whether the effect has shrunk.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the term or mechanism at all
Claiming it's used identically across luxury and mass-market brands
No personal view on whether the technique still works today
followUps: What pricing tactic do you think has replaced or supplemented charm pricing recently?

question: If a global fashion brand were entering a new international market, how much of its marketing strategy should stay the same, and how much should be adapted locally?
lookingFor: Structured thinking about the balance between brand consistency and cultural localisation, with a concrete example.

bullets: Distinguish what should stay consistent (core identity, quality promise) from what should adapt (imagery, language, channel mix, sizing or seasonal relevance)
Give a concrete example of a brand that localised well or poorly
Show awareness that local regulation, culture, and infrastructure all affect the answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the core identity, what the brand actually stands for and its quality promise, needs to stay consistent, because that consistency is what builds trust internationally in the first place. But the execution around it, the imagery used, the influencers partnered with, even things like sizing charts and seasonal timing, needs real local adaptation, since a winter collection launch timed for the northern hemisphere makes no sense entering a market like Australia. A brand I think got this wrong early on is one I read about that translated slogans literally into a new market and lost the actual meaning, which is a reminder that localisation is about intent, not just translation. Getting that balance right seems like one of the genuinely hardest problems in international marketing, and it's part of what makes it interesting to me.

commonMistakes: Arguing for either total standardisation or total localisation with no nuance
No concrete example to ground the reasoning
Ignoring practical factors like regulation, seasonality, or local infrastructure
followUps: What's one thing you'd research first before advising on entering a specific new market?
